newsitem.title: USA: Doctors who listen have fewer lawsuits - study.
newsitem.headline: Doctors who listen have fewer lawsuits - study.

text.p: Doctors who listened to patients' questions and asked them to elaborate on how they felt had fewer malpractice suits than impatient colleagues, researchers said Tuesday.

Researcher Wendy Levinson tape-recorded patients' visits to 120 primary care physicians in Oregon and Colorado. Her research confirmed past studies showing that patients who suffered "bad outcomes" were less likely to sue their doctors if their bedside manner was caring and compassionate.

Levinson, formerly of Oregon Health Sciences University and Legacy Good Samaritan Hospital in Portland, said physicians with less than two malpractice claims took their time during routine patient visits, spending a little more than 18 minutes with each person compared to 15 minutes by doctors who had two or more lawsuits.

In her article in the Journal of the American Medical Association, Levinson gave examples of helpful comments doctors could make: "First I'll examine you and then we will talk the problem over," or "I will leave time for your questions."

She also said humour was useful, adding that some physicians made facilitative statements such as, "Go on, tell me more about that," "What do you think caused that to happen?" and "What do you think about taking these pills?"
